intro: Willem Mengelberg conducts the Concertgebouw Orchestra in the first movement, Allegro con brio, of Beethoven’s Symphony No. 5 in C minor, Op. 67. This is the first of two disc sides, which runs from the four-note opening in octaves to the soft exchanges of the development; the movement continues on the second side.

sections.label: A · Opening motif, three Gs, fermata
sections.mNote: The opening rhythm passes through the strings.

sections.label: B · Horn call and violin melody
sections.mNote: E♭ major; repeated notes continue beneath the melody.

sections.label: C · Opening rhythm in fragments
sections.mNote: Short phrases pass between strings and winds.

sections.label: D · Single chords between winds and strings
sections.mNote: Winds and strings take turns before the rhythm returns.

cues.title: Opening motif and fermatas
cues.text: Beethoven begins with a rest, three Gs and an E♭ held under a fermata. Three Fs then fall to a longer D. Mengelberg has two written pauses to shape before the strings begin passing the rhythm between them.
cues.evidence: Beethoven, Symphony No. 5, I, bars 1–21; Mutopia 941, based on the Breitkopf & Härtel parts. Opening repeated notes, fermatas and subsequent string imitations.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Horn call, bars 59–70
cues.text: The horns play the three-short-note rhythm with wider intervals: B♭–B♭–B♭, E♭, F, B♭. The violins follow with a melody in E♭ major. Below it, the cellos continue the repeated-note figure.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 59–70; Mutopia 941, horns, first violins and cellos. Passage at the recording’s existing second-section boundary.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Telefunken SK 2210, 1941
cues.text: Telefunken issued this performance in 1941. The Concertgebouw Orchestra plays under Mengelberg, and SK 2210 carries the first part of the opening movement. The rest of the movement is on the other side.
cues.evidence: Musical Heritage Organization’s catalogue for Telefunken SK 2210 identifies Mengelberg, the Concertgebouw Orchestra, recording date 1939–40, first release 1941 and first-movement Part 1: http://pool.musicalheritage.org/index.php/Telefunken-sk2210-022110.

cues.title: Development, alternating chords
cues.text: In bars 196–247 the development reduces the four-note rhythm to alternating minim chords. Winds and strings take turns across rests, marked diminuendo and then sempre più piano. The exchanges end when fragments of the repeated-note figure return.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 196–247; Mutopia 941, alternating minim chords, diminuendo, sempre più piano and returning repeated-note fragments. Passage at the existing final-section boundary.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.epithet: Composer known for a symphony built from a four-note motif and for the string quartets of his last years.
facts: Neefe in Bonn; Haydn, Albrechtsberger and Salieri in Vienna
Bonn until 1792; Vienna and its surrounding villages for the rest of his life
Nine symphonies · five numbered piano concertos · 32 numbered piano sonatas · 16 string quartets · Fidelio
Described his hearing loss in 1801; used conversation books from 1818

quote.text: I live only in my notes.
quote.source: Beethoven to Franz Gerhard Wegeler, Vienna, 29 June 1801; our translation

composer.background:
In March 1778 Johann van Beethoven advertised a concert in Cologne by his six-year-old son. Ludwig was seven. His father, a singer in the electoral chapel at Bonn, hoped to launch another child prodigy; his grandfather, also Ludwig, had risen from singer to Kapellmeister in the same establishment. The boy was baptised on 17 December 1770, probably the day after his birth. By his teens he was playing the organ for services and the viola in the court orchestra, where he learned operas as a member of the string section.

Christian Gottlob Neefe put Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier before him and helped him into paid employment. The Breuning household supplied books, friendship and a refuge from Johann’s drinking. After his mother died in 1787, Beethoven increasingly supported his younger brothers. In November 1792 the elector sent him to Vienna to study with Haydn. He was expected to return. French troops occupied Bonn in 1794, and the court that paid him ceased to exist.
